title: Proscription
label: Terrorism Act 2000 · ss.11–13
summary: Once a group is banned, membership and inviting or recklessly expressing support are offences punishable with up to 14 years. Displaying an article is a different, summary offence: six months.
rule: Once an organisation is proscribed, it is an offence to belong or profess to belong to it (section 11), to invite support for it other than by money or other property alone (section 12(1)), or to express an opinion or belief supportive of it while reckless as to whether a person to whom the expression is directed will be encouraged to support it (section 12(1A)). Arranging or addressing a meeting to support the organisation, further its activities, or hear from someone who belongs to it is a further offence (section 12(2) and (3)). It is also an offence to wear or display an article, or publish an image of one, in circumstances that arouse reasonable suspicion of membership or support (section 13).
nuance: The offences are about support for the organisation. Reporting that something happened, quoting words as evidence of an event, or criticising the law that bans a group is not, by itself, an opinion supportive of that group. There is no blanket exemption for material described as reporting. Context and the elements of the particular offence decide it. Where the line falls in a particular case is for a court.

The test in section 12(1A) is recklessness, not intent. A person can commit the offence without meaning to encourage anyone, if they are reckless as to whether a person to whom the expression is directed will be encouraged to support the organisation.

Section 12(1) does not cover an invitation confined to money or other property. That is left to the funding offences. Before 2019, expressing a supportive opinion was an offence only if it invited support or was part of arranging or addressing a meeting. Section 12(1A) and the image offence in section 13(1A), not section 13A, were added in 2019.

The penalties are not the same. Sections 11 and 12 can be tried in the Crown Court: the maximum was 10 years until 29 June 2021, and is 14 years for an offence committed on or after that day. Section 13 is summary only: up to six months, a fine, or both. Many of the sign cases have been charged under section 13, not under the 14-year offence.

Section 11 has a defence. It is for the defendant to prove that the organisation was not proscribed on the last occasion they became a member or began to profess membership, and that they have not taken part in its activities at any time while it was proscribed.

Section 13 does not require proof that the person is in fact a member or supporter. The question is whether the article, in those circumstances, arouses reasonable suspicion. In *Pwr v DPP* the Supreme Court held that section 13(1) is a strict-liability offence beyond deliberate wearing, carrying or displaying, with no further mental element. That holding does not extend to sections 11 and 12. Since 29 June 2026 the uniform offence is not limited to a public place: section 13(1ZA) extends it to prisons and other "relevant premises".

The offences apply only while an organisation is proscribed. The statutory route off the list is an application for deproscription, with an appeal to the Proscribed Organisations Appeal Commission. The Palestine Action case was a different procedure: a judicial review of the decision to make the order. Check the current list on GOV.UK, not a secondary source.
why_it_matters: Proscription turns some acts of expression into terrorism offences, and it applies to people who are not members. Which section is charged decides whether the maximum is six months or 14 years.

history.text: The Terrorism Act 2000 creates the membership, support and uniform offences.
The Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019 adds the reckless-expression offence and the image-publication offence.
The maximum on indictment for membership and for the section 12 support offences rises from 10 years to 14, for offences committed on or after that day. Section 13 stays a summary offence.
*Pwr v DPP*: the Supreme Court holds that section 13(1) does not require knowledge of what the article signifies.
Palestine Action, Maniacs Murder Cult and Russian Imperial Movement are added to the proscribed list.
The High Court proposes to quash the Palestine Action proscription.
The Court of Appeal allows the Home Secretary's appeal; the proscription stands.
Section 13(1ZA) comes into force. Wearing or displaying an article on prison and other "relevant premises" can now be the uniform offence, and a seized article may be destroyed.
